transcript:
Meeting header: Saltlake Health Private VPC egress & inference latency lab
Date: 2028-10-03 16:00 UTC | Duration: ~72 minutes
Attendees: Liam Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Nambiar (Redwood SE), Omar Reyes (Redwood SRE); Arjun Patel (CTO), Maya Rivera (Platform), Ellen Zhou (Security), Jonas Meyer (ML Infra)
Links shared: https://redwood.app/decks/saltlake-egress-lab (deck), https://sheets.example.com/saltlake-benchmarks (bench CSV)

Summary:
Quick lab focusing on Private VPC egress behavior, NAT/hairpin, DNS resolver configuration, MTU retransmit effects on kv-cache throughput, and quantization profile impact on tail latency. Agreed action items and follow-ups captured.

Topics covered:
- PrivateLink vs cross-account peering for inference control plane egress
- Hairpin NAT and registry pulls from on-prem nodes
- DNS stub resolver and conditional forwarding to Saltlake resolver
- MTU mismatches causing TCP retransmits and token-gen tail latency
- KV cache warmup heuristics and prefix caching strategies
- Batching windows vs P99 latency targets
- Int4 quant profiles and quality vs throughput tradeoffs
- KMS/HSM calls during model key unwrap and their latency impact

00:00:12 Liam Chen: All right, thanks everyone for joining. quick intro, I'll hand to Priya for the runtime recap then we can jump into Saltlake's topology.
00:00:28 Priya Nambiar: Hi hi, from Redwood SE — we'll try to run a small lab today, show where we've seen egress hiccups affect token 99s, and propose mitigations. apologies in advance, my audio might clip a bit.
00:00:45 Arjun Patel: No worries. we've had some mid-latency blips when models call out to external endpoints for KMS or metrics. looking to understand whether that's our VPC or runtime kernel selection.
00:01:10 Maya Rivera: for context our pilot runs in a private subnet with no internet egress except via NAT Gateway in a shared services account. we also use AWS PrivateLink for the control-plane.
00:01:36 Priya Nambiar: ok that aligns with setups we've seen. typical places that add tail latency: hairpin NAT when S3/registry pulls happen from same subnet, or MTU fragmentation leading to retransmits.
00:02:05 Ellen Zhou: we also have strict egress rules; any external TLS handshake has to be logged and mTLS to our KMS. we want to avoid breaking PCI-ish flows.
00:02:23 Liam Chen: quick question — are you using the AWS resolver or forwarding to an on-prem resolver?
00:02:32 Jonas Meyer: currently we forward conditional queries to our on-prem DNS over TLS resolver for internal hostnames, AWS resolver for everything else. sometimes the resolver timeouts spike.
00:02:59 Priya Nambiar: that can definitely cause ~100–500ms spikes, especially if the runtime is waiting on external config for routing decisions (e.g., fallback to quantized variant).

00:05:20 Priya Nambiar: demo note — our runtime uses continuous batching and prefix-KV caching. if DNS or NAT delays stall the first token fetch or KV warmup requests, batching windows stretch and P99 increases non-linearly.
00:05:47 Maya Rivera: can you explain prefix-KV warmup — we saw cold-starts where first generation after idle takes 2–3x longer.
00:06:12 Priya Nambiar: yes so we have heuristics where the runtime prefetches KV-cache entries for popular prefixes based on recent traffic. but if those prefetch requests go through an egress path that suffers packet loss or timeout, the warmup misses and subsequent requests hit storage or model compute.
00:07:02 Arjun Patel: is that storage over the network or local disk?
00:07:09 Priya Nambiar: depends — for Dedicated or Private deployments KV can be colocated in-memory on the same host (best). for Saltlake's pilot it's in a managed cache in another AZ behind PrivateLink and that extra hop is visible.

00:09:40 Omar Reyes: quick interjection — we also saw an MTU mismatch between our on-prem appliance and the cloud NAT. large token payloads cause fragmentation and then retransmits; TCP-level retransmits are costly for the long running streams.
00:10:05 Jonas Meyer: interesting — we did observe bursts of retransmits in the flow logs. we assumed it's application-level backpressure but could be network MTU.
00:10:35 Priya Nambiar: yep in practice switching to a consistent MTU (e.g., 1380 for tunneling) or enabling TCP MSS clamping on the NAT reduced retransmits in our internal tests.

00:12:20 Priya Nambiar: let's talk quantization. we've tested int8 and int4 profiles. int4 gives better throughput and lower GPU memory but can add a small delta in model quality and sometimes higher variance in tail latency because kernels are less mature on some hardware.
00:12:43 Maya Rivera: you mentioned kernel selection — how much of that is runtime automatic?
00:12:50 Priya Nambiar: the runtime selects kernels and binding based on model shape, sequence length, and device capability. it may choose different kernels for int4 that trade off latency vs throughput. we also have a 'latency-first' profile that pins CPU/GPU affinity and disables large async batches.

00:15:05 Arjun Patel: if we use PrivateLink for control-plane traffic, what about data-path? we want to keep payloads in Saltlake VPC — ideally direct connect to the inference nodes.
00:15:27 Liam Chen: that is often the pattern: control/control-plane via PrivateLink, model inference stays in-customer VPC or dedicated pool in their region. but some customers still send payloads to the hosted model for rapid iteration — that's when egress and auditing matter.

00:17:00 Ellen Zhou: on compliance, KMS unwraps — do you call our KMS for every model init or is the unwrap cached?
00:17:17 Priya Nambiar: we do a cached unwrap with TTL. the first unwrap is synchronous and can add ~80–150ms; subsequent ones use a cached DEK locally in the runtime for the TTL. but if your KMS endpoint is across a high-latency link, first unwrap is visible in tail metrics.
00:17:52 Jonas Meyer: can we do an HSM/NIC offload or put Redwood's runtime in our private subnet to avoid repeating unwraps over the internet?
00:18:08 Priya Nambiar: yes Private deployment supports customer-managed KMS and HSM integrations; the unwrap path can be local so the latency is bounded by your network.

00:20:30 Priya Nambiar: shared artifact — we uploaded a bench CSV showing int4 vs int8 throughput and P50/P95/P99. link in header. our recommended baseline for pilot is int8 for parity, then int4 for heavy throughput once QA passes.
00:21:10 Maya Rivera: curious about batching windows — we need <200ms P99 for conversational flows. how do we guarantee that with batching?
00:21:36 Priya Nambiar: you can cap batch window to 15ms and apply dynamic sampling to avoid large queue depths; that reduces throughput but keeps P99 lower. we also use hinting: if request has urgent flag, route to latency-first pool with tiny batch size.

00:24:05 Omar Reyes: regarding hairpin NAT: our registry pulls and container image downloads from the same subnet occasionally loop through the NAT in the shared services account causing asymmetric paths and cold-cache registry lookups. any best practices?
00:24:34 Priya Nambiar: avoid hairpin by placing a route to the registry endpoint in the local subnet or use VPC endpoints for S3/ECR so traffic never leaves the VPC. if you must NAT, ensure the NAT has consistent routing and session affinity.
00:25:05 Jonas Meyer: we run an on-prem artifact store that the runtime pulls from; when that store is across a VPN we see delays. should we mirror into a regional S3 behind PrivateLink?
00:25:23 Priya Nambiar: mirroring into a PrivateLink-backed bucket or using a cache node in the same AZ is best. runtime stores model shards in a local cache to avoid repeated pulls.

00:28:10 Priya Nambiar: practical debugging: capture tcpdump on both sides, check TLS handshake times, and inspect flow logs for retransmits. we typically add a 1-minute sampling period at peak to capture P99-generating traces.
00:28:45 Arjun Patel: will Redwood run the same benchmark from our account? we can give temporary access to a test VPC.
00:28:53 Liam Chen: yes we'll run the three benches you requested — int8 baseline, int4 production, and a no-quant test to isolate kernel differences.

00:31:00 Maya Rivera: what about DNS? our conditional forwarder sometimes returns truncated UDP and causes a fallback to TCP, that added ~200ms.
00:31:25 Priya Nambiar: try enabling EDNS0 or increasing response size on the resolver, or force DNS over TLS to avoid truncation. also consider using a stub resolver that keeps TCP warm connections.

00:34:12 Priya Nambiar: another subtlety — KV cache fetches are small but numerous. small UDP/DNS delays multiply because runtime can issue many parallel lookups. consolidating hostnames and using a local resolver cache reduced our observed P99 by 25ms in one test.

00:36:50 Omar Reyes: we noticed SNI mismatches when using PrivateLink endpoints and our proxy did TLS termination — some egress flows were dropped. any recommended SNI/mTLS patterns?
00:37:09 Priya Nambiar: where possible use PrivateLink-specific hostnames and preserve SNI. avoid terminating TLS at a proxy that rewrites SNI unless it re-injects the original hostname. for strict mTLS, use certs pinned per service and mutual auth at the PrivateLink endpoint.

00:39:40 Jonas Meyer: curious — how does the runtime fall back if a batch's KV fetch fails? is there a fallback to a model variant?
00:39:56 Priya Nambiar: yes we have tiered fallbacks: first, retry KV fetch with jitter up to X times; second, fall back to a compatible non-quantized model variant if available; third, if the request is latency-critical we return partial tokens with a note. policies are configurable per route.

00:42:20 Priya Nambiar: let's walk through a quick repro we ran: we injected 1% packet loss on egress and saw P99 increase from 180ms to 620ms, and batching window increased from 12ms to 42ms as more requests queued.
00:42:46 Maya Rivera: 1% loss caused that big of an effect?
00:42:51 Priya Nambiar: yes because the runtime's retransmit/backoff hits the KV fetch and some kernel calls stall on the first tokens, and then the batching window tries to fill to amortize cost leading to higher tail.

00:45:05 Arjun Patel: do you have logs or trace example we can use?
00:45:12 Priya Nambiar: yes attached in the sheet — we included a trace with timing breakdown: DNS 35ms, TLS handshake 120ms, KMS unwrap 90ms, KV fetch 20ms, model kernel 12ms per token.

00:47:30 Omar Reyes: anything we can tune on the NAT side? we use AWS NAT Gateway, can't change firmware of course.
00:47:45 Priya Nambiar: consider using NAT fleet with consistent affinity, enable TCP keepalive tuning, and set MTU/MSS clamp. if possible use egress VPC endpoint for services to keep traffic local.

00:50:00 Maya Rivera: can Redwood preload KV cache during rollout so the first few requests hit warmed caches?
00:50:18 Priya Nambiar: yes we can run a warmup job that simulates common prefixes; for large models we recommend staged rollouts where the canary has a warmup trigger.

00:52:33 Priya Nambiar: thing to watch: quantized kernels for int4 on some GPU families are optimized for throughput; their single-token latency can vary. if your workload is many short chats, int8 or latency-first kernels may be better.

00:55:00 Liam Chen: time check — about 17 minutes left. any security concerns we should cover?
00:55:13 Ellen Zhou: we need an audit trail for KMS unwrap calls and token-level redaction for logs. also RBAC for who can trigger a warmup job that could exfiltrate model shards.
00:55:35 Priya Nambiar: Redwood's private deployment offers audit logs and fine-grained RBAC. warmup jobs run under a service principal and we can limit their scope. we also support token-level scrubbers in the logging pipeline.

00:58:12 Priya Nambiar: propose next concrete bench plan: 1) baseline from Saltlake VPC using current NAT+resolver, 2) baseline with DNS forwarded to local stub resolver, 3) baseline with MTU clamp and PrivateLink-mirrored bucket. Redwood runs benches and shares CSV.
00:58:45 Arjun Patel: agreed. we'll open a temporary test VPC peering and share flow logs and a packet capture.

01:01:20 Priya Nambiar: last bit on observability — we instrument token timing in the runtime and emit per-token spans. that helps isolate whether delay is in kernel, KV, or network. we can share a sample tracing dashboard.
01:01:46 Jonas Meyer: would love that dashboard.

01:04:12 Liam Chen: recap — Redwood to run benches, share PrivateLink diagram and quant tradeoff doc, Saltlake to share captures and enable test VPC access. schedule follow-up week after results.
01:04:40 Maya Rivera: ok we'll aim to have captures by Monday.
01:05:08 Ellen Zhou: also we'll list the compliance artifacts required for the pilot.
01:05:20 Liam Chen: perfect. thanks everyone. we'll send follow-up with clear next steps and link to bench results.

Action items (verbatim from call):
- Priya to prepare int4 vs int8 chart and tradeoffs.
- Omar to try MTU repro and summarize results.
- Redwood to run three benchmark variants from Saltlake test VPC.
- Saltlake to provide packet captures and flow logs.

End of transcript.
